 Inspiration 

 Most browser agents still have to inspect a page, infer what controls mean, and simulate clicks. That approach is fragile, and it gives the web application very little control over how its capabilities are exposed to an AI agent. 

 At the same time, giving an agent unrestricted permission to change real application state creates another problem: useful autonomy can quickly become unsafe autonomy. 

 ActGeX explores a different contract between humans, agents, and web applications: 

 AI agents should be able to analyze, recommend, and act — while humans remain in control of consequential changes. 

 Personal finance is our demonstration environment because it makes that trust boundary easy to understand. An agent can safely analyze spending, but changing a real financial goal should remain a human decision. 

 

 What it does 

 ActGeX is a WebMCP-native financial workspace where a human and an AI agent operate on the same live application state. 

 The application exposes eight typed WebMCP capabilities: 

 
 query_transactions 
 get_category_summary 
 compare_spending_periods 
 flag_unusual_spending 
 recommend_budget_goal 
 simulate_budget_change 
 set_budget_goal 
 export_report 
 

 These tools support a complete agent workflow rather than isolated tool calls. 

 ActGeX's Agent Mission can: 

 
 read transaction data 
 summarize spending 
 compare periods 
 detect unusual spending 
 recommend a budget goal 
 simulate its financial impact 
 present the proposed change to the human 
 apply it only after explicit approval 
 

 For example, the agent can identify that Dining spending increased, recommend a new target, and simulate how that target would affect monthly savings. 

 But the recommendation itself does not silently change the application. 

 When set_budget_goal is requested, ActGeX opens a Human Approval Required dialog showing the proposed change and its Before/After impact. 

 Only after the human explicitly approves does the real application state change. 

 The agent recommends. The human decides. 

 

 How we built it 

 ActGeX exposes application capabilities through WebMCP using: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool has: 

 
 a stable semantic tool name 
 a clear description 
 typed input parameters 
 validation 
 execution logic connected to real application state 
 

 The application is built with: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 Zustand 
 DuckDB-Wasm 
 WebMCP 
 

 The human UI and WebMCP tools operate on shared application state. 

 There is no separate agent-facing copy of the financial workspace. 

 ActGeX also exposes an Agent Financial Context so the agent-visible context is understandable from the human interface itself. 

 The workspace includes dedicated sections for: 

 
 Overview 
 Agent Mission 
 Tools 
 Shared State 
 Approvals 
 Executions 
 Agents 
 Settings 
 

 Shared State makes the live financial data visible as the common state used by both the human and the agent. 

 Approvals surfaces human-owned budget goals and recent approval/rejection decisions. 

 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent often has to reason about visual controls or DOM structure and simulate user interaction. 

 ActGeX changes that model. 

 Instead of asking the agent to locate the correct button or infer the meaning of a UI element, the application exposes semantic capabilities directly. 

 The agent calls capabilities, not pixels. 

 That improves reliability, but more importantly, it lets the application define its own trust boundary. 

 ActGeX can explicitly decide: 

 
 what the agent may read 
 what the agent may analyze 
 what can be simulated safely 
 what requires human authorization before mutation 
 

 WebMCP therefore becomes more than an automation interface. It becomes part of the application's permission and collaboration model. 

 

 Human + Agent collaboration 

 ActGeX is designed around a shared financial state. 

 The human sees the same transactions, budgets, summaries, recommendations, and decisions that the agent operates on. 

 The core interaction loop is: 

 Shared State → Agent Analysis → Recommendation → Simulation → Human Approval → State Change → Activity History 

 This is visible directly in the product. 

 The Agent Mission shows the agent's analysis sequence. 

 The Recommendation explains: 

 
 What should change 
 Why the agent recommends it 
 What impact the change may have 
 

 The Approval dialog shows the Before/After financial effect. 

 The Activity Timeline records agent executions and human decisions. 

 The goal is not invisible automation. 

 The goal is visible collaboration with explicit authority boundaries . 

 

 Human authority 

 ActGeX provides human control over agent behavior. 

 The application supports Observe and Assist authority modes. 

 In Observe mode, the agent can inspect and analyze financial state without making consequential changes. 

 In Assist mode, the agent can perform analysis and prepare recommendations, while consequential state changes still pass through the human approval boundary. 

 The most important example is set_budget_goal . 

 The agent may request the change, but it cannot silently commit it. 

 The user sees the recommendation and simulated impact before choosing whether to approve or reject it. 

 This makes human authority part of the application workflow rather than an external safety policy. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the hardest problems was deciding where agent autonomy should stop. 

 Reading transactions, comparing periods, identifying anomalies, and simulating scenarios are fundamentally different from changing a real financial goal.
